studyDesign: VCE Physics Study Design (Units 1 and 2: 2016-2022; Units 3 and 4: 2017-2023)
note: Accredited VCAA study design used for VCE Physics Units 3 and 4 examinations from 2017 to 2023 inclusive, sourced directly from VCAA's own published study design document (2016PhysicsSD.pdf, Updated version 1.1, 'FOR USE IN 2023'). This is structurally different from the current 2024-2027 design, most notably: relativity (time dilation, length contraction, muon decay) sits in Unit 3 Area of Study 3 here ('How fast can things go?', alongside Newton's laws, circular/projectile motion, and energy/momentum), not in Unit 4 as it does from 2024 onward; and Unit 4's photoelectric-effect/de-Broglie/wave-particle-duality content is split across two areas of study (wave behaviour of light, then light-matter similarities) with a third area of study dedicated entirely to the student-designed practical investigation. See study-design-2024-2027.json for the current design this superseded.

units.title: How do fields explain motion and electricity?

areasOfStudy.title: How do things move without contact?
keyTopics: field model for gravitation, magnetism and electricity
field shapes and directions, attractive/repulsive effects, dipoles and monopoles
gravitational and electric fields about a point mass/charge: direction, shape, inverse square law, qualitative potential energy changes
magnetic fields of bar magnets, current-carrying wires, loops and solenoids
static vs changing fields; uniform vs non-uniform fields
electric field acceleration of a charge: F = qE, W = qV, E = V/d
magnetic force on a charged particle: F = qvB (perpendicular or parallel v and B)
radius of the path followed by a low-velocity electron in a magnetic field: r = mv/(qB)
gravitational field and force: g = GM/r^2, Fg = Gm1m2/r^2
force due to gravity and normal reaction force for satellites in orbit (uniform, circular)
modelling satellite motion (artificial, Moon, planet) as uniform circular orbital motion
interaction of two fields: attraction/repulsion of charges, poles and current-carrying conductors vs mass-only attraction
force on a current-carrying conductor: F = nIlB
simple DC motors: one coil free to rotate in a uniform field, split-ring commutator
particle accelerators: linear acceleration by a uniform electric field, direction change by a uniform magnetic field

areasOfStudy.title: How are fields used to move electrical energy?
keyTopics: magnetic flux: Phi = B*A (field perpendicular to area), qualitative effect of differing angles
generation of emf: AC voltage, induced emf epsilon = -N(delta Phi / delta t) — rate of change of flux, number of loops, direction of induced emf
DC generators (split-ring commutator) vs AC alternators (slip rings)
sinusoidal AC voltage from uniform rotation of a loop: frequency, period, amplitude, peak-to-peak voltage/current
root-mean-square (RMS) voltage/current compared to constant DC voltage delivering the same power
converting between RMS, peak and peak-to-peak values
ideal transformer action: V1/V2 = N1/N2 = I2/I1
transmission losses across transmission lines
advantage of AC as a domestic power supply

areasOfStudy.title: How fast can things go?
keyTopics: Newton's three laws of motion: coplanar forces along a straight line and in two dimensions
uniform circular motion in a horizontal plane: Fnet = mv^2/r — vehicle on a circular road, vehicle on a banked track, object on a string
natural and artificial satellite motion modelled as uniform circular motion
Newton's second law applied to circular motion in a vertical plane (highest and lowest positions only)
projectile motion near Earth's surface, including qualitative effect of air resistance
conservation of energy and momentum in isolated systems, one dimension
Einstein's postulates of special relativity: laws of physics same in all inertial frames; speed of light constant for all observers
comparing special relativity with classical (Newtonian) physics
proper time (t0) and proper length (L0)
time dilation: t = t0*gamma; length contraction: L = L0/gamma
Lorentz factor gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)
explaining why muons reach Earth's surface despite their short half-life (relativistic muon decay)
impulse in an isolated system for straight-line collisions: F*delta t = m*delta v
work done by a constant force: force x distance, and as area under a force-distance graph
kinetic energy Ek = 1/2 m v^2; elastic and inelastic collisions and conservation of kinetic energy
strain potential energy: area under a force-distance graph; ideal springs and Hooke's Law: Es = 1/2 k(delta x)^2
gravitational potential energy: Eg = mg*delta h, or from area under a force-distance/field-distance graph
mass-energy equivalence: Etot = Ek + E0 = gamma*m*c^2, E0 = mc^2, Ek = (gamma - 1)mc^2
nuclear fusion in the Sun converting matter to energy and emitting electromagnetic radiation

units.title: How can two contradictory models explain both light and matter?

areasOfStudy.title: How can waves explain the behaviour of light?
keyTopics: a wave as the transmission of energy through a medium without net transfer of matter
transverse vs longitudinal waves
amplitude, wavelength, period and frequency of waves
wave speed, frequency, wavelength and period: v = f*lambda = lambda/T
constructive and destructive interference from two coherent sources: path difference n*lambda and (n - 1/2)*lambda
qualitative explanation of the Doppler effect
resonance as superposition of a travelling wave and its reflection; forced oscillation matching natural frequency
standing waves in strings fixed at one or both ends
diffraction as directional spread of waves, effect of gap width or obstacle size, qualitative effect of the wavelength/gap-width ratio
light as an electromagnetic wave produced by accelerating charges (changing E and B fields)
all electromagnetic waves travel at speed c in a vacuum
the electromagnetic spectrum: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, x-ray, gamma — wavelength/frequency comparison and uses
polarisation of visible light and its relation to the transverse wave model
refraction: Snell's Law n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2), n1 v1 = n2 v2
total internal reflection and critical angle: n1 sin(theta_c) = n2 sin(90 deg)
colour dispersion in prisms and lenses via refraction of different wavelengths
Young's double slit experiment: evidence for the wave-like nature of light, path-difference interference, effect of wavelength/slit separation/screen distance on fringe spacing (delta x = lambda*L/d)

areasOfStudy.title: How are light and matter similar?
keyTopics: effect of gap width or obstacle size on the diffraction pattern produced by light; limitations for imaging
the photoelectric effect as evidence for the particle-like nature of light
photoelectric-effect data: graphs of photocurrent vs electrode potential, and kinetic energy of emitted electrons vs frequency
kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons: Ek max = hf - phi (work function), in joules and electron-volts
effect of incident light intensity on the emission of photoelectrons
limitations of the wave model of light in explaining the photoelectric effect
electron diffraction patterns as evidence for the wave-like nature of matter
distinguishing between diffraction patterns produced by photons and by electrons
de Broglie wavelength of matter: lambda = h/p
momentum of photons and of matter of the same wavelength: p = h/lambda
atomic absorption and emission line spectra, including metal vapour lamps
photon energy from spectral transitions: delta E = hf
absorption of photons by atoms: change in electron energy levels; frequency/wavelength of emitted photons E = hf = hc/lambda
quantised atomic states explained via electrons forming standing waves — evidence for the dual nature of matter
single photon/electron double-slit experiment as evidence for the dual nature of light and matter
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle illustrated via single-slit diffraction
why classical physics is not appropriate to model motion at very small scales
production of light in lasers, synchrotrons, LEDs and incandescent lights

areasOfStudy.title: Practical investigation
keyTopics: student-designed practical investigation related to waves, fields or motion, with at least two continuous independent variables
independent, dependent and controlled variables
scientific research methodologies and techniques of primary qualitative and quantitative data collection
precision, accuracy, reliability and validity of data; distinction between uncertainty and error
health and safety guidelines
organising, analysing and evaluating primary data: patterns, relationships, sources of uncertainty/error, limitations
models and theories, their use and limitations in explaining observed phenomena
nature of evidence that supports or refutes a hypothesis, model or theory
scientific poster presentation conventions: terminology, representations, symbols, equations, units, significant figures, referencing
